doctrines/sexuality-marriage/question: What is marriage, and how should Christians order sexuality, celibacy, family and gender?
doctrines/sexuality-marriage/summary: From Jesus’ teaching on divorce and celibacy to the sacrament of matrimony, clerical celibacy, the Reformers’ married clergy, divorce and annulment, contraception, polygamy in African churches, gender roles, same-sex relationships and abortion, Christians have repeatedly debated the meaning of marriage and the body. This section presents each view in its own best terms, with its strongest critics.
doctrines/sexuality-marriage/longText:
Christianity inherited from Judaism a high view of marriage as a creation ordinance: "male and female created he them", the two becoming "one flesh". Jesus sharpened it by forbidding divorce, Matthew adding an exception for porneia, and he also commended celibacy "for the kingdom of heaven’s sake". Paul preferred celibacy for undivided service but called marriage a "great mystery" of Christ and the Church. In a Roman world that tolerated abortion and infant exposure, the Didache and the apologists condemned both. As monasticism spread, Jerome ranked virginity above marriage, while Augustine defended the three goods of marriage: offspring, fidelity and sacramental bond.

East and West then went different ways. The Council in Trullo (692) kept married parish priests in the East. The Gregorian reform and the Second Lateran Council (1139) imposed celibacy on Latin clergy. Western theology counted marriage among the seven sacraments and held it indissoluble except by nullity. Byzantine canon law, following Basil, allowed penitential remarriage by "economy". The Reformers rejected compulsory celibacy, married, and treated marriage as a holy covenant and civil estate. Following Erasmus they permitted divorce for adultery and desertion. Trent answered with a sacramental, indissoluble marriage and required public weddings.

Modern questions multiplied. In Africa, missionaries and converts argued over whether polygamists could be baptised, from Bishop Colenso (1862) to Lambeth 1988. The Anglican Lambeth Conference of 1930 first accepted contraception, and Paul VI’s Humanae Vitae (1968) reaffirmed the Catholic prohibition. Evangelicals divided between complementarian and egalitarian views of gender, a debate linked to women’s ordination. After Roe v. Wade (1973) abortion became a defining public issue: most churches upheld the early Christian prohibition, while some mainline bodies defended legal choice. Since the 1990s same-sex relationships have been the most divisive question of all. The historic view, still held by the great majority of the world’s Christians, and the affirming view, adopted by a number of Western mainline churches, are both set out here in their own best terms. The section also follows the outcomes: Lambeth 1998, the Anglican and Methodist realignments (2003–2024) and the Catholic declaration Fiducia Supplicans (2023).
doctrines/sexuality-marriage/flow/nodes/: What is marriage, and how should Christians order sexuality, celibacy, family and gender?

Jesus quoted Genesis — "they twain shall be one flesh" — and forbade divorce, yet praised those who renounce marriage for the kingdom. Is marriage a sacrament, a covenant or a civil estate? May clergy marry? When, if ever, may the married divorce and remarry? Is contraception permitted? How should churches respond to polygamy, to different understandings of men’s and women’s roles, to same-sex relationships and to abortion?
Creation: male and female, one flesh (Gen 1:27–28; 2:18–25)

Humanity is created "male and female" in God’s image and blessed to be fruitful; the man and woman become "one flesh". Patriarchs practise polygamy (Abraham, Jacob, David) and the Law regulates divorce (Deut 24:1–4). Traditional and affirming readers both start here but draw different conclusions about what is normative.
Jesus on divorce and celibacy (Matt 5:31–32; 19:3–12; Mark 10:2–12)

"What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder"; remarriage after divorce is adultery, Matthew adding "except it be for fornication" (porneia). Some are "eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake". Each tradition’s divorce teaching hinges on these verses.
Paul on marriage, celibacy and household (1 Cor 7; Eph 5:21–33)

Paul prefers celibacy for undistracted service but says "it is better to marry than to burn"; spouses owe each other conjugal rights; a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse "is not under bondage" (the "Pauline privilege"). Ephesians calls marriage a "great mystery" (sacramentum in the Vulgate) concerning Christ and the Church.
Texts on same-sex intercourse (Lev 18:22; 20:13; Rom 1:26–27; 1 Cor 6:9–11; 1 Tim 1:10)

Traditional readers see a consistent prohibition grounded in creation; affirming scholars argue these texts address exploitative, cultic or excess-driven practices (pederasty, temple prostitution) rather than committed, faithful same-sex partnerships unknown to the ancient authors. The meaning of arsenokoitai and of "nature" (physis) in Romans 1 is disputed.
Gender in Christ and in the church (Gal 3:28; 1 Cor 11:3–16; 14:34–35; 1 Tim 2:11–15)

"There is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus"; women pray and prophesy in Corinth; Phoebe is a deacon and Junia "of note among the apostles" (Rom 16); yet "I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man". Complementarians and egalitarians weigh these texts differently.
Didache and Athenagoras: no abortion, no exposure (c.100–177)

The Didache’s moral catechism commands: "you shall not murder a child by abortion nor kill that which is born". Athenagoras (c.177) argues that Christians, who call abortion murder and refuse to expose infants, cannot be the killers pagans accuse them of being.
Tertullian: the happiness of Christian marriage (c.200)
Tertullian describes marriage blessed by the church and confirmed by the Eucharist, while urging widows not to remarry: early Christianity both honoured marriage and exalted continence.
Jerome: virginity above marriage (393)

With the rise of monasticism, Jerome ranks virginity, widowhood and marriage as hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold fruit; Jovinian, who denied virginity’s superiority, is condemned at Rome and Milan (c.393).
Augustine: the three goods of marriage (401)

Against both Manichaean contempt for the body and Jovinian, Augustine defends marriage’s goods of offspring, fidelity and sacramental bond, while viewing concupiscence as a wound of the fall: the framework of Western teaching on marriage and sex.
Eastern married clergy (Council in Trullo, 692)

The Byzantine church permits men married before ordination to serve as priests and deacons, reserving the episcopate to celibates (monks); Oriental Orthodox and Church of the East practice is similar, and the East Syriac church once allowed bishops and post-ordination marriage.
Orthodox oikonomia: penitential remarriage (Tome of Union, 920)

Byzantine canon law, following Basil, permits divorce for adultery and other grounds and, by "economy", up to three marriages, the second and third with a penitential rite; marriage is a sacramental mystery whose death can be recognised with sorrow.
Second Lateran Council: clerical marriages invalid (1139)

The Gregorian reform culminates in a ruling that priests’ marriages are not merely forbidden but invalid; Latin clerical celibacy becomes universal law, though concubinage remains widespread for centuries.
Marriage as one of the seven sacraments (1184–1439)

Scholastic theology lists matrimony among seven sacraments (Peter Lombard, c.1150; Council of Verona, 1184; Second Council of Lyon, 1274; Florence, 1439): the consent of baptised spouses makes a sacramental, indissoluble bond signifying Christ and the Church.
Protestant reformers: marriage as covenant and civil estate (1520s)

Luther calls marriage a holy "worldly thing" under civil jurisdiction, not a sacrament; Calvin and the Reformed describe it as a covenant before God; Anglicans keep it as a sacramental rite though not a "sacrament of the gospel". Marriage courts pass to the state.
Reformation clergy marry (1520s–1549)
Zwingli, Luther (marrying the former nun Katharina von Bora in 1525), Bucer and Cranmer marry; the Protestant parsonage becomes a cultural institution. England legalises clerical marriage in 1549.
Erasmian view: divorce and remarriage for adultery and desertion

Following Erasmus’s annotations (1519), Protestant churches permit divorce with the right to remarry for adultery and, in many cases, wilful desertion (Westminster Confession 24.5–6), while urging reconciliation.
Trent defines marriage (Session 24, 1563)

Trent affirms marriage as a true sacrament, declares that the bond is not dissolved by adultery (worded so as not to condemn the Greek practice), and in the decree Tametsi requires a priest and witnesses for validity, ending clandestine marriage.
Catholic indissolubility and annulment

A ratified and consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power; tribunals may declare a marriage null if a true bond never existed (lack of consent, impediments, form). Pope Francis simplified nullity procedures (2015) and opened discernment on communion for remarried divorcees (Amoris Laetitia, 2016).
Colenso and the polygamy question in Africa (1862)

Bishop Colenso argues that polygamous Zulu converts should be baptised with their wives; Henry Venn’s CMS and most missions insist on monogamy before baptism. Many African Initiated Churches later accept polygamous members, and African theologians debate polygamy as a pastoral and cultural question.
Lambeth accepts contraception (1930)
Anglican bishops allow contraception for morally sound reasons; most Protestant churches follow over three decades, while Pius XI’s Casti Connubii (1930) reaffirms the ban.
Humanae Vitae (1968)

Paul VI reaffirms that artificial contraception is intrinsically wrong; John Paul II’s Theology of the Body (1979–84) develops a personalist defence; surveys show most Western Catholics do not follow the teaching, while it finds new defenders among some evangelicals and in Africa.
Abortion after Roe v. Wade (1973)

Legal abortion in the West divides Christians: Catholic, Orthodox, evangelical and Pentecostal churches teach that unborn life must be protected (with differing exceptions), while some mainline Protestant bodies support legal access as a matter of conscience. The Religious Coalition for Reproductive Choice (1973) and the evangelical-Catholic pro-life alliance both form.
Pro-life and "consistent ethic of life" positions

Building on the Didache and the Fathers, Catholics (Joseph Bernardin’s "consistent ethic of life", 1983; John Paul II’s Evangelium Vitae, 1995) and evangelicals (Francis Schaeffer and C. Everett Koop’s Whatever Happened to the Human Race?, 1979) oppose abortion as the taking of innocent human life.
Complementarianism (Danvers Statement, 1987)

The Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood holds that men and women are equal in dignity but called to different, complementary roles, with male headship in the home and male eldership in the church.
Egalitarianism (Christians for Biblical Equality, 1989)

CBE’s statement "Men, Women and Biblical Equality" (1989) argues that gifts, not gender, determine ministry and that marriage is a partnership of mutual submission (Eph 5:21); it links to the movement for women’s ordination.
The historic Christian sexual ethic

From the early church onward, Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teaching held that sexual intercourse belongs only within marriage between a man and a woman, and that same-sex sexual acts, like all sex outside marriage, are contrary to God’s will; celibacy and chastity are the calling of the unmarried.
Revisionist scholarship and gay Christian voices (1955–1980)

Derrick Sherwin Bailey’s Homosexuality and the Western Christian Tradition (1955) re-reads Sodom as about inhospitality; the Metropolitan Community Church is founded (1968); John Boswell’s Christianity, Social Tolerance, and Homosexuality (1980) argues the medieval church was once more tolerant. Critics dispute much of this historical reconstruction.
Affirming view: blessing faithful same-sex relationships

Affirming Christians argue that the biblical texts do not address loving, committed same-sex partnerships, that the fruit of such relationships shows the Spirit’s work (Acts 15 as precedent), and that the church should bless and marry same-sex couples and ordain LGBTQ people.
Lambeth 1998, Resolution I.10

The Anglican bishops, led by a large Global South majority, reject homosexual practice as incompatible with Scripture and decline to advise same-sex blessings, while committing to listen to gay and lesbian people.
Denominational divisions (2003–2024)

The consecration of Gene Robinson (2003) leads to GAFCON (2008) and the Anglican Church in North America (2009); the ELCA (2009), PC(USA) (2011, 2014) and Church of Scotland move toward affirmation, prompting departures; the United Methodist Church divides (2019–2024); the Church of England authorises prayers of blessing (2023) while not changing its doctrine of marriage.
Fiducia Supplicans (2023)

The Catholic Church allows non-liturgical blessings of couples in irregular situations, including same-sex couples, without changing its doctrine of marriage; the African bishops (SECAM) collectively decline to apply it, illustrating global fault lines.
Today: who holds what?

Catholic and Orthodox churches teach marriage as a sacrament between a man and a woman; Catholics keep Latin clerical celibacy (with married Eastern Catholic and convert clergy), annulment and the ban on contraception, while the Orthodox permit married priests, penitential remarriage and, in many places, contraception within marriage. Most Protestant churches see marriage as covenant, permit divorce on limited grounds and accept contraception. On same-sex relationships the large majority of the world’s Christians (Catholic, Orthodox, most evangelical, Pentecostal and Global South churches) hold the historic view, while a growing number of mainline Protestant churches in Europe and North America bless or marry same-sex couples. Complementarian and egalitarian views divide evangelicals; abortion remains opposed by most churches and accepted in law by some mainline bodies.
